section.title: Neetcode: Google vs Amazon, Interviews, and Quitting Big Tech
section.deck: Neetcode describes a short Amazon stint, a move into full-time content creation, and the view that enjoyment and sustained practice matter more than raw LeetCode talent.

blocks.text: Neetcode describes a short first job at Amazon, a move into full-time content creation, and the view that enjoyment and sustained practice matter more than raw talent in interview performance. Much of the conversation tests the common belief that passing big-tech interviews requires solving the hardest LeetCode problems.
blocks.heading: A practical view of interview preparation

blocks.question: What happened after the first full-time job offer at Amazon, and why did Neetcode leave so quickly?
answer: The Amazon role came soon after college, around age 22. Neetcode had expected a hard environment but found the culture a shock. The team had about five new grads who joined in the same month, and several burnt-out mid-level and senior engineers. Neetcode says the team was unfriendly and that most people left within about a year.
Neetcode says the decision to quit after a couple of months was a poor one, made without a backup plan or savings, though it worked out. Neetcode would not recommend it to most people.

followups.question: What did you see at Amazon that made you want to quit so quickly?
answer: Neetcode separates intense high-performing teams, where people compete and still root for each other, from cutthroat teams where people do not. The Amazon team felt like the second kind. Icebreakers were cold, and nobody seemed to be rooting for anyone else.
Neetcode stresses the limit of that judgment. Neetcode was there for only a short time and cannot say whether people tried to harm each other.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

followups.question: What gave you the confidence to quit so quickly?
answer: Neetcode calls the decision uncharacteristic. Shortly before starting at Amazon, Neetcode had been broke and felt on top of the world. Within the first day, the manager signalled that the team was burnt out, and the situation seemed to get worse steadily.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Did the Amazon job require LeetCode-style interviews?
answer: Neetcode says the LeetCode questions were surprisingly easy, close to variations of the two-sum problem. The leadership principles interview was the harder filter. Neetcode admits giving answers that matched the company's picture of a high-agency, risk-taking employee, although Neetcode is naturally risk-averse and careful about mistakes.
Neetcode says the real work at Amazon asked for much higher initiative than expected, and adjusting to that took time.

followups.question: Did a recruiter's logic-puzzle assessment resemble the Amazon screen?
answer: The host recalls a group logic-puzzle test with multiple-choice pattern questions. Neetcode says a similar online test was part of the process, though only one section of it.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Could Neetcode solve the hardest LeetCode problems today?
answer: Probably not. Neetcode says Neetcode was never especially strong at LeetCode. The skill spectrum is compressed on LeetCode, so strong and very strong solvers look similar to most observers. Codeforces, by contrast, spreads skill over a wider distribution.
Neetcode still knows the core patterns and could usually say what the solution would be. Writing it by hand under time pressure would be harder, since few people hand-type code now.

followups.question: What percent of LeetCode medium problems could Neetcode solve now?
answer: Neetcode would be curious to try, and would not solve all of them. For most mediums, Neetcode could explain the pattern or the answer.
The host notes that an impromptu whiteboard session with hard problems was recorded separately and not included in this conversation.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Where does someone who passes interviews fall on the LeetCode and Codeforces skill scale?
answer: Neetcode says the answer is wide. Passing an interview requires competence and some luck in being asked a problem the candidate already knows. Neetcode does not think there is one average candidate, and believes the average is lower than many people think.

Neetcode estimates that solving about a third of LeetCode mediums gives a good chance of passing an interview. A college competition illustrated the spread. One strong teammate solved three of 13 hard problems, while the Caltech team solved all 13.

followups.question: Does a competitive programmer's skill transfer to complexity theory?
answer: The host suggests that competitive programming sits above LeetCode. Neetcode answers that practice transfers less than people expect. Training for one format does not guarantee performance in another, and communication can suffer in a real interview.
Neetcode also says making videos consumed much of the time that might have gone into improving problem-solving, so the videos were a partial distraction.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: What share of LeetCode performance comes from memorization rather than derivation?
answer: Neetcode guesses at least 90 percent is memorization, and considers that acceptable given how much material interview preparation covers. Neetcode notes that pure memorization is not enough. Candidates still need enough understanding to choose between approaches, such as depth-first or breadth-first search.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Is LeetCode an accurate measure of intelligence?
answer: Neetcode says definitely not. Tests such as the SAT correlate with other traits, but LeetCode measures a narrow subset of skill. A dog could not solve these problems, which shows they are not general intelligence.

Neetcode believes the main bottleneck is sustained enjoyment, passion, and work ethic. Neetcode did not do anything exceptional. Neetcode kept making LeetCode videos when most people would not have been willing to put in the time.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: What kept Neetcode making LeetCode videos for so long?
answer: Neetcode says school computer science classes often stopped just as topics became interesting, leaving Neetcode wanting to go ten times deeper. LeetCode videos felt productive, even though views were modest and income was not expected.
Neetcode continued out of stubbornness, enjoyment, and a belief that the videos helped people.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Can anyone become good at LeetCode?
answer: Neetcode believes most programmers who enjoy programming could reach that level. Many people feel they are not smart enough, and many give up along the way because they find the grind unpleasant or prefer other routes, such as networking into a job. Neetcode regards that choice as reasonable.

followups.question: Should some people simply give up on LeetCode?
answer: Neetcode says Neetcode does not recommend giving up. The video came from frustration with a dismissive attitude toward effort, and Neetcode believes people can do more than they think.

Neetcode says about 95 percent of people who clicked on the video liked it, and many said they needed the message. One viewer preparing for a Microsoft internship interview said the video helped them lock in for the next few weeks.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Was the 'give up' video the frustrated response of a disappointed teacher?
answer: Neetcode accepts that description and says it would not make sense to teach people while telling them to quit. Neetcode says the wording was not the nicest. The worst part, in Neetcode's view, was calling one question dumb. The remark was not personal, and Neetcode did not call anyone unintelligent.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Were you worried about how the rant video would be received before posting it?
answer: Neetcode watched it a couple of times before posting and was unsure whether to send it. The rant was not planned. Looking back, Neetcode says it ran through five tangents, and a version designed to go viral would have been tighter.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: How did the video career lead to the Google job?
answer: Neetcode hoped that someone would eventually arrange an interview and that Neetcode would do well in it. It took almost a year. The offer came from Google, which Neetcode says felt like a dream job. The interview felt manageable thanks to heavy preparation.

Google's team was friendly and the work technical, but it was sometimes boring and process-heavy. Neetcode felt that the chance to go full-time on the channel and algorithms would not last, so Neetcode left, though Neetcode says it could have been done sooner.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Which companies ask the hardest LeetCode questions?
answer: Neetcode says the AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, ask demanding questions that do not follow the traditional LeetCode format. Neetcode attributes difficulty mostly to supply and demand: how many people apply and how many roles are open. Neetcode believes smaller companies are often harder.

followups.question: How do OpenAI and Anthropic run their coding interviews?
answer: Neetcode has heard mixed reports. Knowledge of data structures and algorithms still helps. Interviews may include parts of an algorithm, several files, or an open problem to reason through rather than a classic LeetCode task.

Neetcode's understanding is that the Anthropic interview does not allow AI assistance, and that the most recent OpenAI candidate Neetcode spoke with reported the same. Neetcode says some candidates mention AI access, and finds the formats unpredictable.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: Were you nervous about showing your face on the channel?
answer: Neetcode was faceless for the first three years of the channel and began showing a face about three years ago. Being recognized created chances to meet viewers and other creators. Neetcode says part of Neetcode liked the faceless version because it allowed a private, introverted life, but Neetcode has no regrets.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: How has quitting Google to work full-time gone?
answer: Neetcode says it was easier because Neetcode enjoyed the work. Building a site, making videos, and studying algorithms all fit. Neetcode says people who dislike their jobs but do not know what else they want have a harder time.
Neetcode reports no regrets, and says quitting is not for everyone. Neetcode does not buy into the idea that everyone should leave a job for a side business.

followups.question: Does Neetcode miss Google?
answer: Neetcode misses the free food and, more, the culture of a large company. Running Neetcode's own channel made it possible to hire people and shape a culture, which Neetcode enjoyed. Neetcode describes the work as problem solving rather than culture building, and says the management load has been more than expected.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

followups.question: What did Neetcode dislike most about Google?
answer: Neetcode found the company very slow. Urgency and speed did not seem to matter, which is pleasant for work-life balance but frustrating for ambitious people who want projects shipped or promotions. Neetcode says Google placed processes and engineers' feelings ahead of customer impact, the opposite of Amazon in that respect.
followups.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: What is the top technical book recommendation for software engineers?
answer: Neetcode recommends Designing Data-Intensive Applications. Neetcode acknowledges that many readers do not retain the details, but says the book changes how readers think about systems. Neetcode finds parallels to LeetCode problems in almost every chapter and says the book is not for everyone.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode

blocks.question: If Neetcode could advise a younger self just after college, what would it be?
answer: Neetcode would focus more on what they enjoy. Neetcode chose a job that was expected to be reasonably enjoyable and assumed any technical role would do. Neetcode learned web development because it seemed popular, but found it boring. A less common field such as operating systems or databases would have suited Neetcode better.
Neetcode says the same is true of LeetCode. It seems hard to some people, but Neetcode found it easy because Neetcode enjoyed it. The advice is to try to enjoy the work at least a little.
blocks.speaker: Neetcode
